extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, and educated readers interested in the principles and practice of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for practising disinterested, effective literary criticism and for poets on the relation between criticism and creative work; explains what criticism should do, how it supports creativity, and what habits to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: See the object as it really is
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of the critical power is, 'in all branches of knowledge...to see the object as in itself it really is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should aim at clear-sighted, accurate apprehension of its subject across theology, philosophy, history, art, science. By honestly discerning and stating what is best in thought and work, criticism helps establish an order of ideas that creative writers can use. (Quoted phrasing and the generalizing claim are presented as the fundamental task of criticism.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness (keep aloof from the practical view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism's rule may be summed up in one word — 'disinterestedness.' It must keep aloof from the 'practical view of things' and the ulterior practical or political ends attached to ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be a free play of the mind on its subjects, refusing to subserve party, sect, or political aims. Its business is to know and make known 'the best that is known and thought in the world' with 'inflexible honesty, with due ability,' leaving questions of practical application to others. Examples: avoid turning reviews into organs of party interest (Edinburgh, Quarterly, Times cited as cautionary examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from parties and organs with practical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: A true criticism must not be the minister of sects or parties nor subordinate play of mind to their practical business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing criticism that primarily promotes an institutional or political agenda. The essay contrasts independent organs (like the Revue des Deux Mondes) with partisan British reviews and calls for a criticism 'absolutely and entirely independent' to attain real authority and create a current of fresh ideas. The extinction of the Home and Foreign Review is used as an example of how non‑practical criticism can fail commercially though it showed 'play of mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and ability; avoid false or malicious criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism must be written 'with inflexible honesty, with due ability' and false or malicious criticism should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A false or malicious critique does real harm and should not be written. The text contrasts Wordsworth's low estimate of criticism (calling malicious criticism injurious) with the claim that honest, able criticism is valuable. Criticism must be candid but fair, not vindictive. Scoring note: veracity and competence are essential evaluative dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide materials and an intellectual atmosphere for creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical power supplies the ideas and order of thought that the creative power needs; without sufficient materials (ideas current at the time) creative literary genius cannot produce enduring masterworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism's work is preparatory and enabling: by making the best ideas prevail and forming an 'intellectual situation' or atmosphere, criticism readies the 'moment' in which creative genius can synthesize those ideas into great literature. Examples: Goethe benefited from German critical culture; earlier English poets lacked such an atmosphere in Arnold's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism as synthesis-maker, not mere discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern literary genius chiefly performs synthesis and exposition rather than discovering wholly new ideas; it works happiest when inspired by a current intellectual atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should cultivate and clarify the 'order of ideas' current in society; the creative artist then combines and makes beautiful use of these materials. Thus criticism should prioritize identifying and strengthening the best contemporary ideas available to authors rather than obsessing about novelty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets/creators must know life and the world before treating them
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet ought to know life and the world before dealing with them in poetry; modern complexity makes this knowledge require significant critical effort behind the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative work without thorough understanding of contemporary ideas and life will be 'comparatively poor, barren, and short‑lived.' The essay uses Byron, Shelley, Wordsworth vs. Goethe to illustrate that abundant creative energy without adequate critical grounding leads to weakness or incoherence. Practical guidance: read, study, and engage critically with the world before attempting major creative synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading can create a preparatory atmosphere when a national 'current of ideas' is lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a live, national intellectual atmosphere is absent, broad reading and combined critical effort can create a semblance of that atmosphere to nourish poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books and learning are only valuable insofar as they help construct the materials for creative work; they can simulate the permeating intellectual life of great epochs and thus prepare authors and readers for creative flourishing. Example: German culture's collective learning supplied Goethe's milieu; reading can approximate that when society lacks it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid two dilettante extremes (Goethe): neither mere sentimentality nor mere mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe distinguishes two kinds of dilettanti: one neglects the indispensable mechanical part and relies on spirituality/feeling; the other seeks poetry merely by mechanism, acquiring artisan's readiness but lacking soul and matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should beware both extremes. Good art requires both technical mastery (mechanics) and soul/content. The first kind ('neglecting mechanics') most harms art; the second harms the artist personally. Practical implication: cultivate craft and feeling together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer preserving and transmitting the practice of poetry (regulative laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: If poets cannot attain mastery now, they should at least prefer the art to themselves and 'transmit to [successors] the practice of poetry, with its boundaries and wholesome regulative laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not bewilder or waste posterity by abandoning standards or capriciously rejecting tradition; maintain the discipline and rules of poetic practice so future generations can produce 'excellent works.' This advocates conservatism in preserving artistic technique and regulative norms until a future creative epoch arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should correct self-satisfaction and ideal complacency
rubrics_metrics.description: One spiritual use of criticism is to keep people from self-satisfaction that is 'retarding and vulgarizing' by making minds dwell upon what is excellent in itself and the absolute beauty and fitness of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should confront and expose the ideal imperfections behind boastful or complacent rhetoric (examples: contrasting triumphant civic boasts with the grim realities like workhouses and child murder). By presenting such contrasts criticism leads toward perfection and widens spiritual horizon rather than indulging partisan praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing practical/polemical attachments to stifle intellectual play
rubrics_metrics.description: When practical considerations cling to criticism, they 'stifle' it and make it subordinate; such polemical criticism narrows vision and prevents speculative considerations of ideal perfection from reaching people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should resist turning to immediate political or party warfare; when criticism is used to secure practice against attack it produces a narrow, unfruitful sphere. Example: political replies that exaggerate claims (e.g., 'the best breed in the world') are reinforced rather than corrected by partisan criticism. The corrective is candid, disinterested intellectual engagement.
